svg.title: TICKETMASTER: sketchnote
svg.text: Millions of people arrive for one on-sale, and no seat may ever be sold twice.
Browsing is huge, read-only traffic that can
be slightly stale: cache it hard.
Hold a seat with one atomic conditional
update so two buyers can never both win.
For huge on-sales, a virtual waiting room
admits users at the rate the system can
Book tickets: pick seats, hold, pay, confirm
Browse and search highly available, low latency
Extreme spikes: ~10M users for one on-sale
Reads are massive; successful bookings are
Protect the booking path from the read storm.
v1: check, then book (and why it breaks)
The check and the write are separate
steps, so both requests pass the check.
Naive: check the seat is free, then insert a booking. Two users
read "free" at the same time and both book: write skew.
Hold atomically: UPDATE tickets SET status=HELD,
The user pays with Stripe; the idempotent webhook
flips HELD → BOOKED. An expired hold frees itself,
For hot on-sales, a virtual waiting room admits users in
batches; the CDN serves pages and Elasticsearch
handles search, keeping the booking DB small and safe.
Two users click the same seat?
A conditional update on the ticket row (the seat row materializes the conflict, DDIA
Ch 7). Exactly one gets 1 row updated.
The expiry is part of the condition, or a Redis TTL. No background job is needed for
Waiting room queue (Redis sorted set by arrival), push "your turn" via SSE, admit at
Cache for a few seconds; the booking path is the source of truth.
